source: Kulik & Fletcher (2016) Effectiveness of Intelligent Tutoring Systems: A Meta-Analytic Review
finding: Intelligent tutors beat conventional teaching in 50 controlled evaluations. Gains were bigger on locally built tests than on standardized tests.
numbers: 50 evaluations; median effect +0.66 SD (50th to 75th percentile). Six studies with nonconventional controls and four with flawed implementations showed small effects.
limits: ERIC abstract only (full paper not read). Test-instruction alignment inflates effects. Most tutors are in well-structured domains, not open fault diagnosis.
agent_relevance: Expect tutor-style scaffolds to look strong on matched tests and weaker on transfer tests. Evaluate the agent on held-out fault types, not only the trained ones.

source: Ma, Adesope, Nesbit & Liu (2014) Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Learning Outcomes: A Meta-Analysis
finding: ITS beat large-group teaching, other computer instruction and textbooks. ITS did not beat one-to-one human tutoring.
numbers: 107 effect sizes, 14,321 participants. g=0.42 vs teacher-led large group; 0.57 vs non-ITS computer instruction; 0.35 vs textbooks; -0.11 vs individual human tutoring (n.s.); 0.05 vs small group (n.s.).
limits: ERIC abstract only. Effects positive at all school levels and with or without student-misconception modelling, which hints that detailed student models add little.
agent_relevance: A good step-by-step guide is worth about a human tutor, no more. The agent's scaffold should aim for tutor-level step feedback, not elaborate learner models.

source: Johnson et al. (1992) Application of Cognitive Theory to the Design, Development, and Implementation of a Computer-Based Troubleshooting Tutor
finding: Aviation students who added a troubleshooting tutor to the normal course located faults better than controls. They did not detect faults better.
numbers: N=34 (16 control, 18 tutor). Four faults inserted in an aircraft electrical board. Control solved fewer than half of attempted problems; tutor group solved 72%. No difference in recognizing that a fault existed, and no difference on a written electrical-systems posttest. Tutor group evaluated systems before choosing a strategy, used more than one strategy, made fewer misinterpretations and recovered from errors better.
limits: ERIC abstract only. Small N, one school, one board. The written knowledge test did not move: the gain was in procedure, not declarative knowledge.
agent_relevance: Training effect sits in strategy and error recovery, not facts. This supports strategy-choice and recovery operators in the scaffold rather than more knowledge.

source: Johnson & Chung (1999) The Effect of Thinking Aloud Pair Problem Solving (TAPPS) on the Troubleshooting Ability of Aviation Technician Students
finding: Pairs thinking aloud while using the troubleshooting tutor did better than a control group on skill, training efficiency, competence and confidence.
numbers: Effect sizes and N not in the abstract (not read).
limits: ERIC abstract only. No numbers, so treat as direction only.
agent_relevance: Verbalising reasoning to a partner helps trainees. A second model that questions the first (critic pairing) is a close analogue.

source: Westerdahl (1991) The Effects of Expert Systems Training versus Content-Based Training on the Troubleshooting Performance of Novices
finding: Novices given expert troubleshooting methods and a problem-space map solved a task faster than novices given content only.
numbers: Two curricula on a generator-set course; pre and post tests. Result described as faster solution by the expert-method group. No numbers in the abstract.
limits: ERIC abstract only. Author says it is unclear whether the extra knowledge or the extra procedure caused the gain.
agent_relevance: Teaching expert procedure plus a map of the problem space helps novices. The knowledge-versus-procedure confound is unresolved.

source: Katz & Hall (1997) Cognitive Task Analysis and Intelligent Computer-Based Training Systems: Lessons Learned from Sherlock, Hydrive, Eaglekeeper
finding: Pitt and Air Force tutors for F-15 maintenance built coaching and post-problem reflection from a task analysis called PARI (Precursor, Action, Result, Interpretation).
numbers: Evaluation groups: 18 tutored novices, 23 untutored novices, 13 master technicians. Authors report the two finished tutors improved student performance.
limits: ERIC abstract only; effect sizes were not in the record I read. The third tutor (Eaglekeeper) was unfinished.
agent_relevance: The unit of feedback is a full reasoning step: goal, action, result, interpretation. Check that each logged step in our scaffold records all four.

source: Jonassen & Hung (2006) Learning to Troubleshoot: A New Theory-Based Design Architecture
finding: Proposes a troubleshooting learning environment with a layered system model, a simulator that forces hypothesis generation and testing, and a case library with a case-based reasoning engine giving stories from experienced troubleshooters.
numbers: No experiment reported. Claims older methods (domain theory or fixed procedures) failed to produce transferable skill.
limits: Architecture proposal; evidence is cited from other work. The 'failed to transfer' claim is not tested here.
agent_relevance: This is the design the case-library idea comes from: hypothesis step, simulator, then retrieved stories. Our agent can copy the three parts.

source: Hernandez-Serrano & Jonassen (2003) The Effects of Case Libraries on Problem Solving
finding: Undergraduates given a library of related stories while solving ill-structured problems were compared with comparable and control groups.
numbers: Multiple-choice and short-answer tests; groups: experimental, comparable, control. Numbers not in the abstract.
limits: ERIC abstract only; I could not see effect sizes. The library held stories, not machine faults.
agent_relevance: Only direct test of case libraries in the Jonassen line; numbers still to be found. Treat 'case library helps' as plausible but unquantified for human learners.

source: Lajoie & Lesgold (1989) Apprenticeship Training in the Workplace: Computer-Coached Practice Environment (SHERLOCK)
finding: Sherlock is a coached practice environment for Air Force avionics technicians, compared by the authors with human-coached apprenticeship.
numbers: No numbers in the record.
limits: ERIC abstract only. The widely quoted claim that about 20 hours matched years of experience was not verified by me.
agent_relevance: Treat the famous Sherlock efficiency claim as unverified until the full evaluation report is read.

source: Bastani et al. (2025) Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics (PNAS)
finding: In a school RCT, plain GPT-4 helped during practice but hurt later exam scores. A tutor-prompted GPT-4 (hints, no answers) removed the harm.
numbers: Turkey high school, nearly 1,000 students, four 90-min sessions. Practice scores: GPT Base +48%, GPT Tutor +127% vs control (control mean 0.284 on 0-1 scale, SD 0.287). Exam without AI: GPT Base -0.054 (-17%, p<0.05); GPT Tutor -0.004 (n.s.). 2,848 observations.
quote: students do not perceive any reduction in their learning
limits: One topic (math), one school, GPT-4 in fall 2023. Students did not notice their own learning loss.
agent_relevance: Scaffold must withhold the answer and guide. A memory that hands over whole solved cases may act like GPT Base. Hint-style case use is safer.

source: Kestin et al. (2025) AI tutoring outperforms in-class active learning: an RCT (Scientific Reports)
finding: A prompt-engineered AI tutor with worked-solution scaffolding beat in-class active learning in a Harvard physics course, in less time.
numbers: N=194 undergraduates, crossover design. Post-test higher for AI group, p<1e-8; linear regression effect size 0.63, called an underestimate because of ceiling effect. Students spent less time and reported more engagement.
limits: One course, short-term post-test, ceiling effect. The tutor had expert step solutions in its prompt.
agent_relevance: Giving the model a verified solution as hidden reference makes the tutor accurate. A case library with checked solutions plays the same part.

source: Wang, Ribeiro, Robinson, Loeb & Demszky (2024, v3) Tutor CoPilot: A Human-AI Approach for Scaling Real-Time Expertise (RCT)
finding: Giving tutors real-time LLM suggestions built on expert think-aloud reasoning raised student mastery, most for weaker tutors.
numbers: 900 tutors randomised (450/450); analysis sample over 700 tutors and 1,013 students, 4,136 sessions, 350,000+ messages. Mastery +4 percentage points (p<.01; passing 62% to 66%). Lower-rated tutors +9 points. About $20 per tutor per year. Back-of-envelope +0.024 SD on end-of-year test.
limits: Mastery measured by exit tickets, not the end-of-year test. Tutors said some suggestions were not grade-appropriate. Abstract of v1 said 900 tutors and 1,800 students; v3 text says over 700 and about 1,000.
agent_relevance: Expert-reasoning prompts help the weakest user most. A case or expert-think-aloud library should help weaker base models more than strong ones.

source: Goh et al. (2024) Large Language Model Influence on Diagnostic Reasoning: A Randomized Clinical Trial (JAMA Netw Open)
finding: Giving physicians an LLM did not improve their diagnostic reasoning, although the LLM alone scored higher.
numbers: 50 physicians (26 attendings, 24 residents). Median score per case 76% (LLM-assisted) vs 74% (conventional); adjusted difference 2 points, 95% CI -4 to 8, p=.60. LLM alone: 92%, 16 points above control (95% CI 2 to 30, p=.03).
limits: Small N, vignettes, not machine-fault diagnosis. Humans used the LLM poorly.
agent_relevance: A help can fail when the user does not use it well. For our agent the loop should force use of retrieved cases, not leave it optional.

source: Dogan et al. (2026) The Impact of AI-Supported Instruction on Student Learning in STEM: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis (J Intelligence)
finding: AI-supported instruction in STEM helps achievement on average, with high heterogeneity.
numbers: 35 studies 2005-2025. Random-effects g about 0.67 (p<.001); fixed-effect g=0.593, 95% CI 0.522-0.664; Q=199.76, I2=82.98%. Elementary g=0.465, middle 0.392, university 0.578. Duration 1-2 months g=0.833. Science 0.676, math 0.650, tech/engineering 0.501 (group difference n.s., p=.088).
limits: Mixed AI types, mostly pre-LLM; high heterogeneity; I did not read the publication-bias test results in detail.
agent_relevance: The average hides a wide spread; do not expect a fixed gain. Multi-week use gave the biggest effects.

source: Zhao et al. (2024, AAAI) ExpeL: LLM Agents Are Experiential Learners
finding: An agent that stores past trajectories and distils rules from success and failure pairs beats plain ReAct. Both parts matter.
numbers: ALFWorld ExpeL 59.0% at one attempt vs ReAct 40.0%. HotpotQA ExpeL 39.0% vs ReAct 28.0%. Insights-only / retrieval-only: HotpotQA 36% / 31%, ALFWorld 50% / 55%, WebShop 37% / 38%.
limits: Text environments; gpt-3.5 and gpt-4. No human-case comparison. Some table cells in the extracted text were ambiguous.
agent_relevance: Retrieval of cases plus distilled rules are complementary. Our memory should keep both raw cases and rules.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL ablations on case retrieval and insight quality
finding: Which cases you retrieve matters. Task-similarity retrieval beat random retrieval and reasoning-step similarity. Adding reflections to rule extraction hurt.
numbers: ALFWorld: ExpeL 59.0%, reasoning-similarity 48.5%, random sampled 42.5%, ReAct 40.0%. HotpotQA rules: hand-crafted 32.0%, with reflections 29.0%, gpt-3.5-written 32.0%, ExpeL 39.0% (ReAct 28.0%). Extracting insights from only the few-shot examples gave no gain over ReAct; an experience pool built with Reflexion retries beat one built with ReAct alone.
limits: The mapping of table rows to numbers is my reading of extracted text.
agent_relevance: Random cases barely help (42.5 vs 40.0). Retrieval quality is the part to test. Failure and success pairs give better rules than success lists alone.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL transfer and retry results
finding: Rules from HotpotQA transferred to FEVER, and ExpeL combined with Reflexion retries kept improving.
numbers: FEVER: ReAct 58%; transferred-rule agents 63% to 70% (row labels unclear in extraction). ALFWorld with retries: ReAct+Reflexion 40.3, 47.8, 52.2, 54.4 over R0-R3; ExpeL+Reflexion 59.0, 60.4, 63.4, 64.2.
limits: Transfer was to a near-identical Wikipedia task.
agent_relevance: Transfer holds between close tasks; do not expect rules from one fault family to cover another.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Agent Workflow Memory (AWM)
finding: Reusable workflows induced from past runs raised web-agent success, even across templates and domains.
numbers: WebArena (gpt-4): 35.5% vs BrowserGym 23.5% (+12.0 points, +51.1% relative), about 2.0 fewer steps. Beat human-written-workflow SteP by 7.6% relative. Mind2Web cross-task step success 45.1 (offline) / 43.6 (online) vs MindAct 36.2; cross-domain 32.6 / 35.5 vs 18.6.
limits: Online workflows from wrong predicted runs can hurt; offline helps when training matches test; gains smaller across websites.
agent_relevance: Induce reusable procedures from cases, not only store cases. Online induction generalises better across domains.

source: Zhou et al. (2025) Memento: Fine-tuning LLM Agents without Fine-tuning LLMs (case-based reasoning memory)
finding: A case bank of past successes and failures, used without weight updates, gave top deep-research results and gains out of distribution.
numbers: GAIA validation 87.88% Pass@3, test 79.40%. DeepResearcher 66.6 F1 / 80.4 PM. Case memory adds +4.7 to +9.6 points on out-of-distribution sets (MuSiQue, Bamboogle, PopQA). Over five iterations: no CBR 78.65 to 84.47; non-parametric CBR 79.84 to 84.85; parametric CBR 80.46 to 85.44.
limits: The CBR gap shrinks to about 1 point by iteration 5; the case bank saturates quickly (about 3k training items).
agent_relevance: Case library gives early gains that fade as the set is learned. Small curated memory is the target.

source: Zhou et al. (2025) Memento: effect of number of retrieved cases K
finding: A few retrieved cases are enough. More cases do not help and can hurt slightly.
limits: One planner and executor pair (gpt-4.1 + o4-mini). QA, not fault diagnosis.
agent_relevance: Retrieve about 4 cases. Most of the gain comes from the first retrieved case.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) How Memory Management Impacts LLM Agents: An Empirical Study of Experience-Following Behavior
finding: Agents copy retrieved cases when the new task looks like the old one. Bad stored cases spread errors, and even correct-looking cases can mislead.
numbers: Four agent setups. Add-all and coarse selective addition lag an error-free-memory baseline at once and the gap grows; history-based deletion with a strict evaluator can beat the error-free memory baseline in AgentDriver.
quote: error propagation, where inaccuracies in past experiences compound and degrade future performance
limits: Few headline numbers; several agents are synthetic or domain-specific. Evaluator quality drives results: coarse or noisy evaluators make deletion worse.
agent_relevance: A case library needs quality control: score cases by how they did on later tasks and delete the ones that led to failures.

source: Suzgun et al. (2025) Dynamic Cheatsheet: Test-Time Learning with Adaptive Memory
finding: A self-curated memory of strategies and code snippets lifted strong models a lot on some tasks, but small models gained little.
numbers: Claude 3.5 Sonnet AIME 2024 23% to 50%; AIME 2025 +30 points; GPQA-Diamond +9; MMLU-Pro Eng/Physics +8. GPT-4o Game of 24 10% to 99%. Math Equation Balancer to about 98% vs baselines near 50%. Memory-free strong-prompt baseline DC- got 19% on Game of 24.
limits: Large gains are concentrated where one reusable trick (code snippet) solves the task. GPT-4o-mini and Claude 3.5 Haiku benefited little: memory filled with flawed strategies.
agent_relevance: Memory amplifies what the model can already do. The library's value depends on the base model producing some correct cases first.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
finding: Storing a written self-critique of the last failed attempt and retrying raised success on coding, search and household tasks.
numbers: HumanEval pass@1 91% vs GPT-4 80%. ALFWorld +22 points over baseline in 12 trials; HotPotQA +20; self-reflection added 8 points over episodic memory alone.
limits: Memory is a small sliding window. Needs a failure signal (tests or reward). Authors note risk of local minima.
agent_relevance: Failure-to-lesson is a cheap case. It works only when the outer loop gives a trustworthy pass or fail signal.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager: An Open-Ended Embodied Agent with LLMs (skill library)
finding: A library of verified code skills grows an agent's abilities. Without it, progress plateaus.
numbers: 3.3x more unique items, 2.3x longer distances, up to 15.3x faster tech-tree milestones than prior state of the art. Removing self-verification cut discovered items by 73%; random curriculum cut item count by 93%; no skill library plateaued late.
limits: Minecraft; skills are code that can be run and checked. Not troubleshooting.
agent_relevance: Library entries should be verified before storing (self-verification was the most important feedback).

source: Das et al. (2021, EMNLP) Case-based Reasoning for Natural Language Queries over Knowledge Bases (CBR-KBQA)
finding: A neural case memory (question and logical form pairs) lets a model answer new complex questions and use new cases without retraining.
numbers: On ComplexWebQuestions beats prior best by over 11 points accuracy; competitive on WebQSP; uses k=20 cases. A revise step improves accuracy.
limits: Only the abstract and part of the results text were read. Pre-LLM seq2seq model.
agent_relevance: Early evidence that adding new cases at test time works without retraining.

source: Wiratunga et al. (2024) CBR-RAG: Case-Based Reasoning for Retrieval Augmented Generation in LLMs for Legal QA
finding: Structuring retrieval as case retrieval (separate question, support and hybrid similarity) improved legal answer quality.
numbers: Best setting: hybrid AnglEBERT with weights [0.25, 0.40, 0.35], k=3; cosine-score tables show hybrids around 0.90-0.91. Exact gain over plain RAG not recorded.
limits: Metric is embedding similarity to a reference answer, not accuracy; I did not extract a clean headline gain.
agent_relevance: Which part of a case you index on (problem vs solution) changes retrieval quality. Index both separately.

source: Gap note: replication of the human case-library effect (not found)
finding: No independent replication of a case-library benefit for troubleshooting was found in the sources I could reach. VanLehn (2011) human-vs-ITS effect sizes and the Sherlock full evaluation could not be fetched.
numbers: None.
limits: Absence is a reach limit, not proof: web search budget was spent and the OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar and arXiv query APIs were rate limited.
agent_relevance: Do not claim the human case-library effect is replicated.
